newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parliament passes budget for 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: Japan parliament passes budget for 1997/98.

text.p: A state budget criticised for making only half-hearted attempts to cut debt while failing to promote economic recovery became law on Friday when it received approval from the Upper House of Japan's parliament.
The budget for 1997/98, which Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has said will be the first year of fiscal reforms, grew only 3.0 percent from last fiscal year's original budget.
The budget, totalling 77.39 trillion yen ($629 billion), had been passed by the Lower House on March 5.
The 1996/97 original budget had risen 5.8 percent from the previous year.

Although the government has stressed that it is allowing only minimal growth, the budget has attracted much criticism for failing to drastically cut spending while heaping a bigger burden on the public by ending special income tax cuts and raising the consumption tax to five percent from three percent.

The budget also set aside funds to study extending lines for Shinkansen bullet trains, pointing to the possibility of huge spending in the future. Critics said it showed an inflexible approach in sticking to past practices in its allocation of funds for public works projects.

Government officials have been saying that smooth implementation of the budget without delay will help support the current economic recovery, but economists say it is a tight budget that could do more harm than good to the economy.

Hisashi Yamada, an economist at Japan Research Institute, said: "We're running under tight fiscal finances. For example, public works investments fell by around two trillion yen ($16.2 billion) from last year. These things will inevitably work as a negative factor for the economy."

But economists said that with the recovery becoming more solid due to the strength of the private sector and external demand, there will be only a limited impact from the decline in support for the economy that will result from lower public works spending.

"Fiscal measures no longer play a major role in the economy. It's wrong to just look at the fiscal side and think that tighter finances would be bad for the economy," said Susumu Kato, chief economist at BZW Securities Japan Ltd.
"There's hardly any risk of the Japanese economy falling into recession again, although the growth may slow down (temporarily)," Kato said.

Hashimoto pledged last week to cut general spending in the state budget in the fiscal year starting in April 1998 from the previous year, as a way to reduce the state deficit to three percent of annual gross domestic product (GDP) by 2003.
Japan's fiscal deficit for calendar 1997 is seen at around 6.3 percent of gross domestic product, one of the worst levels among major industrialised countries.

Economists said the government's role now ought to be to help nurture the budding strength in the private sector through deregulation, rather than reverting to the traditional remedy of public works projects to support economic growth.

Earlier on Friday, the government finalised a three-year programme to deregulate the economy, comprising 2,823 measures covering areas such as financial services, communications, housing, distribution, transport, energy, labour and education.

But it admitted that only 890 of the measures were new and the rest had already been cited in some form by various government ministries. It also left unclear the timing of when they would be implemented.
